title: Built exactly to sign-off, and the user still said no
explain:
A feature is built exactly to signed-off requirements.

The user rejects it.

The team argues about whether it is a defect, and the argument lasts longer than the fix would have.

Here is how it happens:

→ Feature is built to signed-off requirements
→ User rejects it
→ No one classifies the cause
→ Defect, ambiguity, missed need and scope change are all treated the same
→ The wrong owner works on the wrong fix

The assumption was:
"It matches the sign-off, so it must be right."

Why?

A defect means the build does not match the requirement, an ambiguity means the requirement was read differently, a missed need means the requirement was incomplete, and a scope change means the need has moved. Each cause has a different owner and a different fix.

Each cause has a different owner and a different fix.

BA Takeaway

Classify the rejection first: defect, ambiguity, missed need or scope change. The classification decides the owner and the fix.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Defect
→ Ambiguity
→ Missed need
→ Scope change

The real requirement is not "Was it built to sign-off?"

It is "What evidence proves which of the four causes this rejection is?"

Have you seen a rejected feature argued as a defect when it was really a missed need?
takeaway: Each cause has a different owner and a different fix, so classifying it correctly is the first step.

title: The UAT that tested the system and missed the business
explain:
User acceptance testing is planned for a EUR 110,000 payment release.

The test cases cover the system mechanics.

The business journeys are never tested, and acceptance fails on the first real journey.

Here is how it happens:

→ Test cases are built from system mechanics
→ Business journeys are never mapped
→ Acceptance criteria are never defined per journey
→ Roles that must perform each journey are never identified
→ Exception paths are never covered
→ Tests pass, and the business says no

The assumption was:
"Test the system."

Why?

UAT coverage is derived from the business journeys, the acceptance criteria, the roles involved and the exception paths. Test cases built from this coverage test the business outcome rather than the system mechanics, which is what acceptance testing is for.

Test the business outcome, not the system mechanics.

BA Takeaway

Map each business journey, define the criteria that prove it works, name the roles that must perform it, and cover the exception paths.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Business journeys
→ Acceptance criteria
→ Roles and exception paths

The real requirement is not "Do the tests pass?"

It is "What evidence proves every business journey has a test?"

Have you seen UAT fail on a journey no test ever covered?
takeaway: Test cases built from this coverage test the business outcome rather than the system mechanics, which is what acceptance testing is for.

title: The defect debate that ran on opinion, not evidence
explain:
A system integration testing defect is raised on a EUR 70,000 payment flow.

The discussion runs on opinion for an hour.

Nobody has checked whether the defect can even be reproduced.

Here is how it happens:

→ Defect is raised in SIT
→ Reproducibility is never assessed
→ Traceability to the requirement is never checked
→ Business impact is never assessed
→ Fix validation and regression are never planned
→ The debate runs on opinion

The assumption was:
"The defect is obvious."

Why?

Reproducibility decides whether the defect is real, traceability shows which requirement it breaks, business impact decides its priority, fix validation confirms the fix works, and regression confirms nothing else broke.

Evidence, not opinion, decides a defect.

BA Takeaway

Assess reproducibility, traceability, business impact, fix validation and regression for every defect, in that order.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Reproducibility
→ Traceability and business impact
→ Fix validation and regression

The real requirement is not "Whose opinion is loudest?"

It is "What evidence proves this defect is real, and what it breaks?"

Have you sat in a defect debate that ran on opinion because nobody had checked the evidence?
takeaway: This assessment keeps defect discussions focused on evidence rather than on opinion.

title: Hypercare ended on a date, and the EUR 40,000 exceptions were still open
explain:
A payment release goes live, and hypercare runs for two weeks.

On day fourteen, hypercare ends, because the calendar says so.

EUR 40,000 of exceptions are still unresolved, and nobody is watching them.

Here is how it happens:

→ Deployment goes live
→ Critical journeys are monitored
→ Exception rates are monitored
→ Unresolved transactions are monitored
→ Stakeholder updates go out
→ Hypercare ends after a fixed number of days, while the measures are still unstable

The assumption was:
"Hypercare runs for two weeks."

Why?

Critical journeys show whether customers can complete their payments, exception rates show whether the system is handling failures, and unresolved transactions show what still needs attention. Hypercare ends when these measures are stable, not when a fixed number of days has passed.

Hypercare ends when the measures are stable, not when the calendar runs out.

BA Takeaway

End hypercare on stability, not on a date. Keep monitoring the critical journeys, the exception rates and the unresolved transactions until they hold steady.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Critical journeys
→ Exception rates
→ Unresolved transactions

The real requirement is not "How many days of hypercare?"

It is "What evidence proves the measures are stable enough to end hypercare?"

Have you seen hypercare end on a date while exceptions were still open?
takeaway: Hypercare ends when these measures are stable, not when a fixed number of days has passed.

title: The behaviour changed in production, and nobody knew which layer broke it
explain:
A EUR 50,000 payment behaves differently in production than intended.

The team fixes the code.

The fault was in the requirement, so the fix changes nothing, and the same miss recurs.

Here is how it happens:

→ Intended behaviour diverges from production behaviour
→ Requirement layer is never checked
→ Development layer is blamed by default
→ Testing layer is never checked
→ Environment layer is never checked
→ Fix lands at the wrong layer

The assumption was:
"Fix the code."

Why?

Check the requirement first, then the development, then the testing, then the environment, and find the layer where the divergence was introduced. Locating the layer matters because it decides whether the fix is a requirement correction, a code change, a test improvement or an environment fix.

Fix at the layer that introduced the fault.

BA Takeaway

Use a layered failure model to locate where it went wrong, and fix at that layer.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Requirement layer
→ Development layer
→ Testing and environment layers

The real requirement is not "What is broken?"

It is "What evidence proves which layer introduced the divergence?"

Have you seen a fix land at the wrong layer because nobody traced the fault?
takeaway: Fix at the layer that introduced the fault.

title: The dashboard that said healthy while customers failed
explain:
A digital banking dashboard shows adoption climbing.

The dashboard says healthy.

Customers are failing to complete their payments, and the KPI set never measures it.

Here is how it happens:

→ Adoption is measured, and it climbs
→ Task completion is never measured
→ Failure is never measured
→ Service performance is never measured
→ Risk is never measured
→ Customer outcome is never measured
→ The dashboard reports health while customers fail

The assumption was:
"Adoption is the KPI."

Why?

Key performance indicators should cover adoption, task completion, failure, service, risk and customer outcome measures. Adoption shows whether customers use the feature, task completion shows whether they can finish what they start, failure shows where they are blocked, service shows whether the system performs, risk shows whether controls are holding, and customer outcome shows whether the feature delivered value.

A KPI set that covers only one of these gives a misleading picture of health.

BA Takeaway

Cover all six measures, or the dashboard will report health while customers fail.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Adoption and task completion
→ Failure and service
→ Risk and customer outcome

The real requirement is not "Are customers using it?"

It is "What evidence proves the KPI set shows the whole picture?"

Have you seen a dashboard report healthy while customers were failing?
takeaway: A KPI set that covers only one of these gives a misleading picture of health.

title: The payment page customers kept abandoning
explain:
A merchant watches customers abandon the payment page every day.

The team treats it as one problem with one cause.

It is five problems wearing one label, and each needs a different fix.

Here is how it happens:

→ Customers reach the payment page
→ The funnel shows where they drop off
→ Validation errors block them
→ Latency makes them wait
→ Payment options do not match what they want
→ The experience they report is poor
→ Each cause points to a different fix

The assumption was:
"Abandonment is one problem."

Why?

Customers abandon a payment page for reasons that can be found in the evidence: the funnel, the validation errors, the latency, the payment options and the user experience. The analysis must separate them rather than treating abandonment as a single problem with a single cause.

Abandonment is several problems wearing one label.

BA Takeaway

Separate the five causes before choosing a fix, or the fix will treat the wrong problem.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Funnel drop-off
→ Validation errors
→ Latency
→ Payment options and experience

The real requirement is not "Why do customers abandon the page?"

It is "What evidence proves which of the five causes is driving the drop-off?"

Have you seen abandonment treated as one problem when the evidence showed five?
takeaway: Abandonment is several problems wearing one label.

title: The loan approval that took two days, and nobody knew where the time went
explain:
Loan approval time rises from hours to days.

Everyone has an opinion about where the delay is.

Nobody has measured it.

Here is how it happens:

→ Approval time rises from hours to days
→ The process is never mapped
→ Queues where applications wait are never found
→ Manual checks that add delay are never found
→ Dependencies on other teams are never found
→ Rework where applications are sent back is never found
→ Opinions fill the gap where measurement should be

The assumption was:
"Ask people where the delay is."

Why?

Map the process to find the bottleneck: look for queues, manual checks, dependencies and rework. The bottleneck is usually a queue or a manual step rather than the decision itself, so measuring where time is actually spent is more useful than asking people where they think the delay is.

Measure the clock, not the opinion.

BA Takeaway

Map the process, measure where time is actually spent, and fix the bottleneck the clock shows.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Queues
→ Manual checks
→ Dependencies and rework

The real requirement is not "Where do people think the delay is?"

It is "What evidence proves where the time is actually spent?"

Have you seen a delay blamed on the decision, when the clock showed a queue?
takeaway: Measure the clock, not the opinion.

title: Every test passed, and UAT still failed
explain:
All test cases pass.

UAT still fails.

The suite is green, and the business need is unmet, because the tests never represented the real business journeys.

Here is how it happens:

→ Test cases all pass
→ Test design has gaps
→ Test data does not represent real business use
→ Expected outcomes are wrong
→ The unmet business need was never covered by a test at all
→ Acceptance fails

The assumption was:
"All tests pass, so we are ready."

Why?

Passing test cases do not prove the business need is met. Check the test design for gaps, the representativeness of the test data, the expected outcomes for correctness, and whether the unmet business need was ever covered by a test at all.

Passing tests are not proof. Representation is.

BA Takeaway

Check design, data, expected outcomes and coverage of the real business need before calling a suite ready.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Test design
→ Test data
→ Expected outcomes and coverage

The real requirement is not "Do the tests pass?"

It is "What evidence proves the tests represent the real business journeys?"

Have you seen a green test suite fail acceptance because the tests never matched real use?
takeaway: A test suite that passes but does not represent the real business journeys gives false confidence and a failed acceptance.

title: The same change, requested every sprint
explain:
The same change is requested every sprint.

It is implemented every sprint.

It keeps coming back, because the root cause was never fixed.

Here is how it happens:

→ Same change is requested
→ It is implemented again
→ The unresolved root need is never found
→ Weak discovery missed the real requirement
→ Policy uncertainty leaves the team guessing
→ No one owns the decision, so no one can say no
→ The request returns next sprint

The assumption was:
"Add it to the backlog again."

Why?

The root cause is usually unresolved: an unresolved root need that the change does not actually satisfy, weak discovery that missed the real requirement, policy uncertainty, or a lack of decision ownership. Fixing the root cause stops the repeated request; implementing the same change again will not.

Repeat requests are a symptom, not a backlog.

BA Takeaway

Stop re-implementing and find the root cause: the need, the discovery, the policy or the ownership.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Root need
→ Discovery
→ Policy and decision ownership

The real requirement is not "What change is requested?"

It is "What evidence proves the root need behind the repeated request?"

Have you seen the same change requested sprint after sprint, because the root cause was never fixed?
takeaway: Repeat requests are a symptom, not a backlog.

title: The rule the developers guessed, and the EUR 25,000 payment that proved them wrong
explain:
A rule for a EUR 25,000 payment is stated as a business sentence.

The developer guesses the boundary.

The payment proves the guess wrong, and the rule has to be rewritten after the build.

Here is how it happens:

→ Rule is stated as a business sentence
→ Triggers that start the rule are never stated
→ Conditions that apply are never stated
→ Data involved is never stated
→ Expected behaviour is never stated
→ Failure outcomes are never stated
→ Developer guesses, and the guess is wrong

The assumption was:
"The business sentence is enough."

Why?

A rule stated as a business sentence leaves the developer guessing about the boundary, while a rule stated with triggers, conditions and failure outcomes can be built and tested without further questions.

Precision at the boundary is what makes a rule buildable.

BA Takeaway

State triggers, conditions, data, expected behaviour and failure outcomes for every rule, so it can be built and tested without further questions.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Triggers and conditions
→ Data involved
→ Expected behaviour and failure outcomes

The real requirement is not "What does the rule say?"

It is "What evidence proves the developer can build this rule without asking again?"

Have you seen a rule guessed at the boundary, and the payment prove the guess wrong?
takeaway: Precision at the boundary is what makes a rule buildable.

title: The test that could not pass or fail
explain:
A test is written for a EUR 30,000 payment scenario.

It has steps, but no expected result.

It runs, and nobody can say whether it passed or failed.

Here is how it happens:

→ Business scenario is translated into a test
→ Positive scenario is written
→ Negative scenario is written
→ Boundary scenario is written
→ Regression scenario is written
→ No expected result is stated for any of them
→ The test cannot pass or fail

The assumption was:
"Write the test steps."

Why?

Positive scenarios prove the happy path works, negative scenarios prove invalid input is handled, boundary scenarios prove the limits behave correctly, and regression scenarios prove existing behaviour still works. Each scenario needs an expected result, because a test without an expected result cannot pass or fail.

A test without an expected result cannot pass or fail.

BA Takeaway

Give every scenario an expected result, across positive, negative, boundary and regression coverage.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Positive and negative scenarios
→ Boundary and regression scenarios
→ Expected results

The real requirement is not "Are the test steps written?"

It is "What evidence proves every scenario states what should happen?"

Have you seen a test run that nobody could call a pass or a fail?
takeaway: Each scenario needs an expected result, because a test without an expected result cannot pass or fail.

title: Feature complete, and the business problem still standing
explain:
A feature for a EUR 130,000 payment flow is delivered complete, on time.

The business problem is still there.

The team celebrates delivery, while the users keep working around the problem.

Here is how it happens:

→ Feature is built as specified
→ Hypothesis behind the feature is never revisited
→ Actual user behaviour is never checked
→ Process adoption is never checked
→ Operational constraints are never checked
→ Outcome measures are never checked
→ Delivery is celebrated, and the problem remains

The assumption was:
"Delivery is success."

Why?

The gap is usually that the feature was built as specified but the hypothesis was wrong, or that users did not adopt it, or that an operational constraint was missed. Measuring the outcome rather than the delivery reveals the gap.

Measuring the outcome rather than the delivery reveals the gap.

BA Takeaway

Revisit the hypothesis, the user behaviour, the adoption, the constraints and the outcome measures before calling a feature done.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Hypothesis
→ User behaviour and adoption
→ Constraints and outcome measures

The real requirement is not "Was the feature delivered?"

It is "What evidence proves the feature solved the problem it was built for?"

Have you delivered a feature complete, and watched the business problem stay exactly where it was?
takeaway: Measuring the outcome rather than the delivery reveals the gap.

title: Loan approval: two hours became two days
explain:
Loan approval time grows from two hours to two days.

The team wants to change something, anything.

Nobody knows which of the five causes is actually responsible.

Here is how it happens:

→ Approval time grows from two hours to two days
→ Queue time is never analysed
→ Manual reviews are never analysed
→ Document quality is never analysed
→ Decision rules are never analysed
→ Hand-offs are never analysed
→ A change is made blind

The assumption was:
"Change something, anything."

Why?

Queue time shows where applications wait, manual reviews show where human effort adds delay, document quality shows where rework is created, decision rules show where the logic is slow, and hand-offs show where work is lost between teams. The fix depends on which of these is actually causing the delay.

Measure before changing anything.

BA Takeaway

Analyse queue time, manual reviews, document quality, decision rules and hand-offs, then fix the cause the measurement shows.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Queue time and manual reviews
→ Document quality
→ Decision rules and hand-offs

The real requirement is not "What should we change?"

It is "What evidence proves which of the five is causing the delay?"

Have you seen a fix applied blind, when measurement would have shown a different cause?
takeaway: The fix depends on which of these is actually causing the delay, so measure before changing anything.

title: The change request that came back, again and again
explain:
Stakeholders repeat the same change request, release after release.

It is implemented, again and again.

The cycle repeats, because the cause is never fixed.

Here is how it happens:

→ Same change request is repeated
→ It is implemented again
→ Root need was never satisfied
→ Decision took so long the requester assumed it was ignored
→ Discovery missed the real requirement
→ Feedback loop never closed with the requester
→ The request comes back

The assumption was:
"Implement it again."

Why?

The root need may never have been satisfied, the decision may have taken so long that the requester assumed it was ignored, the discovery may have missed the real requirement, or the feedback loop may never have closed the loop with the requester. Each cause has a different fix.

Implementing the change again without fixing the cause will only repeat the cycle.

BA Takeaway

Investigate the root need, the decision latency, the incomplete discovery and the feedback loops, and fix the cause, not the request.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Root need
→ Decision latency
→ Discovery and feedback loops

The real requirement is not "What change is requested?"

It is "What evidence proves the loop with the requester actually closed?"

Have you seen the same request come back because the loop with the requester never closed?
takeaway: Each cause has a different fix, and implementing the change again without fixing the cause will only repeat the cycle.

title: EUR 50,000 supplier payment stalled, and no one owned the fix
explain:
A EUR 50,000 supplier payment sat unreleased for three days.
Every team said it was someone else's job.
The BA owned the outcome, but no team reported to the BA.

Here's how that happens:

→ pacs.008 held for a missing approval
→ Operations waited for Compliance
→ Compliance waited for the business
→ No one chased the decision, so nothing moved

The requirement said:
"The BA owns delivery."
But ownership came with no authority over any team, no decision record and no date.

Why?

Ownership without authority fails when the ask is vague. Each team assumed another team was acting, and with no recorded decision there was nothing to follow up on and no one to escalate to.

Authority is borrowed. Clarity is owned.

What proves a blocked payment is actually moving again?

BA Takeaway

State what is needed and by when, in writing. Record every decision so accountability is visible. Follow up on actions instead of assuming they will happen. Escalate transparently the moment a decision or a delivery is blocked.

Keep these controls separate:

→ What is needed
→ Who decides it
→ By when
→ What happens if it stalls

The real requirement isn't "When will this be fixed?"

It's "What evidence proves the payment is moving again?"

title: EUR 2 million in payments, and no one could prove where they were
explain:
Volumes tripled in an hour during a payment surge.
EUR 2 million of payments were in flight.
Timeouts rose, and no one could prove which payments had settled and which had not.

Here's how that happens:

→ Volumes tripled in one hour
→ Timeout rates climbed across the gateway
→ Gateway responses mixed success and failure
→ Reconciliation showed gaps nobody could explain

The instruction was:
"Just restart it and see."
Restarting without evidence would have risked paying twice or losing payments entirely.

Why?

Without transaction IDs, gateway responses, API logs, timestamps and reconciliation status, the team was guessing. Each piece of evidence answers a different question, and only together do they show where the money is.

Without evidence, incident response is guesswork.

Collect transaction IDs to link evidence to individual payments. Read gateway responses and API logs to see what each system did. Watch timeout rates to see where the system is struggling. Use timestamps to fix when it happened. Check reconciliation status to see whether the money is accounted for.

→ Transaction IDs
→ Gateway responses and API logs
→ Timeout rates and timestamps
→ Reconciliation status

The real requirement isn't "Is the system back up?"

It's "What evidence proves every payment in the surge is accounted for?"

explain:
A payment of EUR 30,000 timed out.
The team blamed the network and the receiving bank.
The fault was made at the very first step, when the message was created.

Here is what happened:

→ pain.001 created with a small deviation from the payment message standard
→ pacs.008 sent downstream
→ Each hop passes the deviation on
→ Receiving system cannot process it, pacs.002 reports a timeout

The requirement said:
"Validate the message at entry, then trust it downstream."

So the message passed entry checks, and the deviation compounded at every hop until the payment timed out.

Why?

The most visible error is rarely the root cause. A payment timeout is often a downstream effect of something earlier. A small deviation from the standard compounds hop by hop, and by the time the timeout appears, the trail back to the creation step has gone cold unless timestamps and message copies were kept.

The symptom is downstream. The cause is upstream.

BA Takeaway

Creation, each hop and the final timeout are separate evidence points, so keep them separate:

→ Message creation and standards validation
→ Hop by hop trace with timestamps and message copies
→ Timeout symptom, traced back to its origin

Validate messages against the standard at every boundary, not just at entry.

The real requirement is not "Where did it time out?"

It is "What evidence proves the message was valid at every boundary it crossed?"

Have you ever traced a timeout back to a tiny error made when the message was created?
takeaway: The symptom is downstream. The cause is upstream.

title: A EUR 1,500 collection was rejected. The team resubmitted it, and it was rejected again.
explain:
A EUR 1,500 collection is rejected.
The team resubmits it at once, with no timing rule.
It is rejected again, because the resubmission was never tied to the original timing.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 1,500 collection rejected
→ Team resubmits with no timing rule
→ Resubmission rejected again
→ No one can say when resubmission should happen

The requirement said:
"A rejected collection can be resubmitted whenever the team is ready."

Why?

When a collection is rejected, the originator can resubmit it only once the resubmission timing rule is clear, so before asking for the rule, the BA should ask what the rule must answer: how it aligns the original timing so the resubmission improves on the original outcome. The method compares the clean-state timeline of a complete collection with the rejection reason and the proposed resubmission timeline, and tests if the earliest resubmission point is tied to the original collection date. Once the rule is clear it goes into the backlog so the feature can be built quickly, and the BA should first see how the business operation works in practice, face to face.

Define the resubmission timing rule first, then resubmit.

BA Takeaway

Compare the clean-state timeline with the rejection reason, tie the earliest resubmission point to the original date, and write the rule down before building.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Rejection reason
→ Original collection date
→ Resubmission timing rule

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves this resubmission improves on the original outcome?"

Have you resubmitted a collection that was doomed to fail again?
takeaway: Define the resubmission timing rule first, then resubmit.

title: A EUR 45,000 payment came back. The pacs.004 said returned, but nobody knew why.
explain:
A EUR 45,000 payment is returned by pacs.004.
The team knows it was returned, but not why it failed.
The investigation starts from the return alone, and steers the technical team to the wrong process.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 45,000 payment returned by pacs.004
→ Return reason unknown
→ Investigation starts from the return alone
→ Technical team sent to the wrong process

The requirement said:
"A pacs.004 tells you why a payment failed."

Why?

A pacs.004 return tells a bank that a payment was returned, but on its own it does not say why it failed, while the pacs.002 carries the return reason code, and only when the two are reconciled does the bank know whether to flag, retry, investigate, replace or reject the payment. Gap analysis compares the instruction against its structure, the investigation against its evidence, the business rules against their procedure, and the return reason against its expected outcome. It measures the delta between the process the bank has and the process it needs, because a faulty gap analysis steers the technical team toward the wrong process.

Read the reason code, then investigate. Never the other way round.

BA Takeaway

Reconcile the pacs.004 with the pacs.002 reason code before deciding what to do, and measure the gap between the process you have and the one you need.

Keep these controls separate:

→ pacs.004 return
→ pacs.002 reason code
→ Gap analysis

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves why this payment failed, not just that it returned?"

Have you investigated a return without ever reading its reason code?
takeaway: Read the reason code, then investigate. Never the other way round.

title: A EUR 25,000 payment was rejected for a format fault. Reject or repair? The team guessed.
explain:
A EUR 25,000 payment is rejected for a format fault.
The team rejects it again without checking where the fault sits.
The fault was in the bank's own pacs.008, and a mapping fix would have saved the payment.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 25,000 payment rejected for a format fault
→ Fault location never checked
→ Payment rejected outright
→ Fault was in the bank's own pacs.008

The requirement said:
"A format fault always means rejection."

Why?

A payment rejected for a format fault is not always a rejection, because the right response depends on where the fault sits, whether the original instruction is intact, who owns the defect, and whether the agreement permits a correction. When the bank's own pacs.008 is wrong, fix the mapping and repair and resubmit after status and duplicate checks, and when the customer pain.001 is wrong and the agreement allows correction, repair within the agreement and keep the audit trail, while a customer pain.001 fault with no agreement gets a rejection with a clear reason. A format fault is a diagnosis to make first, not a verdict, and the business context decides whether the payment is repaired or rejected.

A format fault is a diagnosis, not a verdict.

BA Takeaway

Locate the fault, check the instruction is intact, check the agreement, then repair or reject with a reason.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Fault location
→ Instruction intact
→ Agreement permission

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves where this fault sits, and whether correction is allowed?"

Have you rejected a payment your own mapping had broken?
takeaway: A format fault is a diagnosis, not a verdict.

title: The EUR 100K limit was removed. A EUR 200,000 payment went to TARGET2 anyway.
explain:
The EU Instant Payments Regulation removes the EUR 100K scheme maximum for SCT Inst.
A customer with a EUR 300K bank limit sends EUR 200,000 instantly.
The old routing rule still sends anything above EUR 100K to TARGET2, and the payment takes the slow road.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 100K scheme limit removed
→ Customer given a EUR 300K instant limit
→ EUR 200,000 sent instantly
→ Old routing rule sends it to TARGET2

The requirement said:
"Removing a scheme limit automatically updates the routing rules."

Why?

When the EU Instant Payments Regulation removed the EUR 100K scheme-level maximum for SCT Inst, the old routing rule that sent payments above EUR 100K to TARGET2 lost the scheme limit it was built on. A bank can now set its own customer limits, so Customer A with a EUR 300K limit can send EUR 200K instantly while the unchanged routing rule still sends anything above EUR 100K to TARGET2, which means two live rules produce different outcomes for the same payment. The BA must surface the conflict, trace why each rule exists, and take the choice to the Product Owner or Business Owner, because only the business can decide which outcome it wants once the scheme constraint is gone.

Two live rules, one payment, two different outcomes.

BA Takeaway

Surface every rule conflict the moment a scheme limit changes, trace why each rule exists, and let the business choose the outcome.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Scheme limit
→ Customer limit
→ Routing rule

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves which rule should win for this payment?"

Have you found two live rules fighting over the same payment?
takeaway: Two live rules, one payment, two different outcomes.

title: The platform handled today easily. Then five new clients arrived, and it fell over at 9am.
explain:
Payment traffic peaks between 7am and 10am, and today the platform copes.
Five clients in the pipeline could add 10 million transactions a month.
Nobody asked when they onboard, what their peaks look like, or whether the workload itself changes.

Here is how that happens:

→ Monthly volume recorded
→ Peak between 7am and 10am never tested
→ Five clients could add 10 million transactions a month
→ Platform fails at the morning peak

The requirement said:
"Monthly volume defines what a platform must support."

Why?

Monthly volume describes scale, but peak behaviour describes performance demand, so a BA who only records today's volumes has not defined what the platform must support. With payment traffic peaking between 7 AM and 10 AM and five clients in the pipeline who could add 10 million transactions a month, the BA must establish when they onboard, how certain the forecast is, what their peaks look like, whether they create new bursts, and whether the workload itself changes with more validations, API calls, real-time processing, and concurrency. The answer is a six-part view of current demand, peak behaviour, future demand, planning horizon, workload characteristics, and measurable requirements that cover response time, processing conditions, volume, and peak TPS, because a platform that performs today can still fail tomorrow if growth was never considered.

Peak behaviour defines performance demand, not monthly volume.

BA Takeaway

Define performance from current demand, peak behaviour, future demand, planning horizon, workload and measurable requirements, and test it at the peak.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Current demand
→ Peak behaviour
→ Future demand
→ Measurable requirements

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves this platform holds at the morning peak with the new clients on board?"

Have you sized a platform on monthly volume and watched it fail at 9am?
takeaway: Peak behaviour defines performance demand, not monthly volume.
